title: Carciofi alla Romana
subtitle: Roman braised artichokes with mint and garlic
excerpt: Carciofi alla romana are globe artichokes stuffed with garlic, fresh mint, and parsley, then braised in olive oil and water until completely tender. The artichokes soften all the way to the centre and the braising liquid becomes a light, herb-flavoured oil to spoon over the top.
sourceNotes: Carciofi alla Romana is one of two classic Roman artichoke preparations, alongside carciofi alla giudia (deep-fried whole). The braised Roman version is stuffed with what Romans call 'mentuccia', a small-leaved Roman mint. Standard garden mint is the closest substitution outside Italy. The dish appears in Ada Boni's Il Talismano della Felicità (1927), one of the foundational Italian cookbooks of the 20th century.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Carciofi alla romana can be made a day ahead. They are equally good at room temperature. Reheat gently in the pan with a splash of water or serve cold.

glossaryTerms.definition: Removing the tough outer leaves, cutting the top third of the artichoke off, and trimming the stem to reveal the pale flesh inside. Work quickly and rub cut surfaces with lemon to prevent browning.

content.text: Carciofi alla romana are globe artichokes braised in olive oil, water, garlic, and fresh mint. The artichokes are trimmed, stuffed with a herb mixture, and cooked upside down in a covered pot for 40 to 45 minutes until they are soft all the way through. The trimming takes time the first few times you do it, but the braising is entirely hands-off.
Fill a bowl with cold water and squeeze in the lemon, then drop the squeezed halves in too.

: snap off the tough dark outer leaves until you reach the paler inner leaves. Cut the top third off. Trim the stem, leaving about 4 cm attached, and peel it with a knife or peeler to remove the tough outer layer. Rub all cut surfaces with lemon immediately. Drop the trimmed artichoke into the lemon water.
Mix the garlic, mint, parsley, a pinch of salt, and 1 tablespoon of olive oil together.
Drain the artichokes. Spread the inner leaves apart gently and push some of the herb mixture down between the leaves and into the centre of each one.
Stand the artichokes stem-up in a saucepan that holds them snugly upright. Pour the remaining olive oil and water into the pan. Season with salt.

Cover with a tight lid and cook over low to medium-low heat for 40 to 45 minutes, checking occasionally. The artichokes are ready when a knife slides easily into the heart and the outer leaves pull off without resistance. If the pan dries out, add a little water.
Serve with the cooking oil spooned over the top. Eat warm or at room temperature.

Roman artichoke cookery has two branches: the braised Roman version and the Jewish-Roman deep-fried version. The braised Roman artichoke is eaten throughout Lazio in spring when the Romanesco artichokes, a large, rounded, thornless variety, are in season. The traditional herb is mentuccia, a small wild mint native to central Italy. Garden mint gives a similar result.
